# 3D Western

3D Western is a student club at Western University that runs free makerspaces for students, in partnership with Morrissette Entrepreneurship. I joined the club's data team in Sep 2025, working on the 3D model scraping and the STL rendering pipeline, and I was VP of Data/ML from May to Aug 2026, alongside my TeraGo internship. The club was building a print service where students submit jobs through its website, and anyone can upload an STL, so it needed a classifier to stop explicit or weapon-like models.

3D Western > tl;dr
(experience, Sep 2025 to Aug 2026, role: Software Developer (Sep 2025 to Apr 2026), then VP of Data/ML (May 2026 to Aug 2026))

- There was no labelled set of 3D models to choose one with, so the data team built one. I wrote the render scripts and got them working with the team's preprocessing pipeline. I rendered and verified the full set and fixed the bugs that broke the run: 2,559 clean labelled models from 4,620 scraped files.
- Our best small local model, Qwen3-VL-2B with the binary_v7 prompt, matched the labels on 84.2% of models with the filename included, and still missed about 21% of what it should flag. Our best image-only number is 76.9%, from the earlier v6 prompt. It isn't ready to ship.
- I built the eval that ruled out Shieldstral, a 3B safety model. Reviewing the pipeline, I noticed it only verified labels we already had, while real uploads arrive unlabelled, so we turned toward classification. I handed off a smoke-tested multi-model benchmark for a cluster run.

3D Western > The team and my role
(experience, Sep 2025 to Aug 2026, role: Software Developer (Sep 2025 to Apr 2026), then VP of Data/ML (May 2026 to Aug 2026))

Alongside the frontend, backend and infrastructure teams, the data team was two VPs and two developers. The other VP was also VP of Backend, so I ended up running most of the day-to-day: reviewing PRs, testing changes locally and getting them merged. It was my first dev team outside two-day hackathons, with the work tracked on a GitHub project board, and I liked working that way.

3D Western > Building the dataset
(experience, Sep 2025 to Aug 2026, role: Software Developer (Sep 2025 to Apr 2026), then VP of Data/ML (May 2026 to Aug 2026))

A teammate's pipeline drops exact duplicates by SHA-256 hash (802), calls my render scripts to render each model in Blender, has a cloud VLM check each render against its scraped folder label, and exports the matches. The scraped folders were safe, unsafe and grey. Unsafe held only nudity, and grey held the other categories we'd want to stop: in the clean set, guns, knives, swords and gestures. For a print gate, both count as "flag".

From 4,620 scraped files to 2,559 clean ones. 1,259 went to review: 735 mismatches, 522 uncertain, and 2 matches that didn't make the export. Two charts. Left, a funnel: 4,620 STL files discovered, 3,818 unique after removing 802 duplicates, and 2,559 in the clean dataset. Right, stacked bars: of the 3,818 checked, 735 were label mismatches and 522 were uncertain. The clean 2,559 split into 1,091 safe, 336 unsafe and 1,132 grey.

My part:

3D Western > Building the dataset
(experience, Sep 2025 to Aug 2026, role: Software Developer (Sep 2025 to Apr 2026), then VP of Data/ML (May 2026 to Aug 2026))

My part:

- I reviewed the branch against its ticket. It met all five acceptance criteria, but every render failed: it asked for Blender's EEVEE_NEXT engine, which doesn't exist in Blender 5.1.1. I switched it to WORKBENCH, which I'd measured at about 3 times faster per view than the Cycles setup in the render scripts.

- I merged it with a teammate's new render branch. It merged cleanly, then broke in four places, which I fixed: the manifest was never written, so contact sheets failed; the preset flag was ignored; grid layouts never cleaned up their tiles; and the contact-sheet glob looked for the wrong filenames.

- I added parallel workers, a resolution flag and output renaming to the batch renderer, then rendered the set with zero failures. Each model became one labelled 768×568 contact sheet of six 256×256 views, about 258 Gemini image tokens, against about 1,032 for the same sheet with 800 px views.

(experience, Sep 2025 to Aug 2026, role: Software Developer (Sep 2025 to Apr 2026), then VP of Data/ML (May 2026 to Aug 2026))

- I added parallel workers, a resolution flag and output renaming to the batch renderer, then rendered the set with zero failures. Each model became one labelled 768×568 contact sheet of six 256×256 views, about 258 Gemini image tokens, against about 1,032 for the same sheet with 800 px views.

- I ran the full verification of 3,818 models. The VLM kept matching the "grey" label to the grey clay of the render, so I made the prompt say labels describe the content. Results were only saved at the end, so one restart cost about 50 minutes of calls; I added per-sample saves and resume.

That first review is also where I noted the pipeline only checks models against labels they already have. Real uploads have none, so production has to classify. I rewrote the production prompt as a classifier around a teammate's taxonomy prompt, the best in a 1,440-call prompt evaluation.

The 2,559-model benchmark set. Unsafe is the nudity folder and grey is guns, knives, swords and gestures. Both count as flag, so 1,468 of the 2,559 (57%) should be flagged. Donut chart of the 2,559-sample benchmark set. Safe 42.6%, guns 33.0%, nudity 13.1%, swords 5.7%, knives 4.2%, gestures 1.4%. Counted as a binary task, 57% is unsafe.

3D Western > Benchmarking small vision models
(experience, Sep 2025 to Aug 2026, role: Software Developer (Sep 2025 to Apr 2026), then VP of Data/ML (May 2026 to Aug 2026))

We wanted a model small enough for the club to run itself, starting with Qwen3-VL-2B. The data team iterated on prompts on a 30-sample dev set, where v5 peaked at 90%. With so few samples, the versions that count are v6 and the later v7, run on all 2,559 clean models.

Every number below is agreement with folder labels a cloud VLM confirmed, so the clean set leans toward models a VLM already recognizes. Prompts and thresholds were chosen on this same set too, with no held-out split, so I'd read all of them as optimistic.

binary_v6 on the clean set, with the filename. It flags 4.2% of safe models and misses 30.7% of the ones it should flag. Dashboard for Qwen3-VL-2B with the binary_v6 prompt on 2,559 samples. Accuracy 80.6%, safe precision 69.9%, false positive rate 4.2%, false negative rate 30.7%, about 1.5 seconds per sample. Per-category accuracy: safe 96%, nudity 81%, guns 67%, knives 48%, swords 70%, gestures 74%. Filename plus size scores 80.6% against 76.9% for vision only.

3D Western > Benchmarking small vision models
(experience, Sep 2025 to Aug 2026, role: Software Developer (Sep 2025 to Apr 2026), then VP of Data/ML (May 2026 to Aug 2026))

binary_v6 on the clean set, with the filename. It flags 4.2% of safe models and misses 30.7% of the ones it should flag. Dashboard for Qwen3-VL-2B with the binary_v6 prompt on 2,559 samples. Accuracy 80.6%, safe precision 69.9%, false positive rate 4.2%, false negative rate 30.7%, about 1.5 seconds per sample. Per-category accuracy: safe 96%, nudity 81%, guns 67%, knives 48%, swords 70%, gestures 74%. Filename plus size scores 80.6% against 76.9% for vision only.

binary_v6 sees the render plus the file's name and size, which scored 80.6% against 76.9% from the image alone. But a scraped filename can give the answer away, and uploaders name files anything, so 76.9% is our realistic baseline.

binary_v7, a later revision, cut misses from 450 to 307 at the cost of more false flags (97, up from 46), and matched the labels on 84.2% of models. It also sees the filename, and these results don't include an image-only run of it.

3D Western > Shieldstral vs Qwen
(experience, Sep 2025 to Aug 2026, role: Software Developer (Sep 2025 to Apr 2026), then VP of Data/ML (May 2026 to Aug 2026))

We kept Qwen3-VL-2B with binary_v7: the highest agreement and less than half of Shieldstral's false flags, for 26 more misses. Two charts on all 2,559 samples. Accuracy: Qwen3-VL-2B binary_v6 80.6%, Qwen3-VL-2B binary_v7 84.2% (kept), Shieldstral-1.0-3B at threshold 0.02 80.7%. Errors: binary_v6 46 false positives and 450 false negatives, binary_v7 97 and 307, Shieldstral 212 and 281.

Shieldstral-1.0-3B is made for image safety. I wrote an eval harness for it on llama.cpp that scores its probability of "yes" from the same render and filename. At the default threshold of 0.5 it got 56.7%. A sweep over the saved scores reached 80.7% at 0.02, again tuned on the same set. It missed 26 fewer than binary_v7 (281 against 307), but it produced more than twice the false flags to review (212 against 97) and it's a bigger model to host, so we kept Qwen.

3D Western > Shieldstral vs Qwen
(experience, Sep 2025 to Aug 2026, role: Software Developer (Sep 2025 to Apr 2026), then VP of Data/ML (May 2026 to Aug 2026))

Shieldstral-1.0-3B is made for image safety. I wrote an eval harness for it on llama.cpp that scores its probability of "yes" from the same render and filename. At the default threshold of 0.5 it got 56.7%. A sweep over the saved scores reached 80.7% at 0.02, again tuned on the same set. It missed 26 fewer than binary_v7 (281 against 307), but it produced more than twice the false flags to review (212 against 97) and it's a bigger model to host, so we kept Qwen.

To see why Shieldstral needed such a low threshold, I ran a small control. A real photo of an AK-47 scored 0.90 for unsafe, and a clay render of an AK-47 part scored 0.20. My best explanation is domain shift: its encoder learned from photos, and clay renders look like generic mechanical shapes. Two images don't prove it, but scoring renders and photos of the same objects across categories would.

3D Western > Handoff
(experience, Sep 2025 to Aug 2026, role: Software Developer (Sep 2025 to Apr 2026), then VP of Data/ML (May 2026 to Aug 2026))

I got all four open PRs merged to main, then reviewed the multi-model benchmark harness and runbook for Nibi, a research compute cluster. I fixed four issues, like a missing path that failed silently, smoke-tested it end to end and handed it off with a 30-sample check to run before the full sweep.

3D Western > What I'd do next
(experience, Sep 2025 to Aug 2026, role: Software Developer (Sep 2025 to Apr 2026), then VP of Data/ML (May 2026 to Aug 2026))

Still open when my term ended in Aug 2026:

- Build a held-out split and rerun v7 on it, with and without the filename.
- Check whether Qwen's saved scores have the same threshold headroom Shieldstral had.
- Sort the flagged models into bad source labels and verifier mistakes, and reuse them as a harder test set.
- Finish the switch to classifying uploads, then wire it into the print form.

# ferret

Local-first semantic file search. Ferret indexes text, images and PDF pages into one local SQLite file and searches it by meaning, keywords or filename, from the terminal, from fzf, from Quickshell or from an agent. It ships as one static Rust binary, with no daemon and no GUI.

ferret > How it works
(project, Oct 2026 (approx.), role: solo)

1. Walk the configured roots, honouring gitignore, hidden files, size caps and include or exclude globs, and report every skip.
2. Extract text chunks, image pixels and PDF pages, the last as text plus an optional raster per page.
3. Embed through an OpenAI-compatible embedding server. The default is a local `llama-server` running EmbeddingGemma; ferret itself never loads model weights.
4. Search hybrid: vector similarity, keyword and filename, fused with reciprocal rank fusion, with filters applied in SQL before ranking.

ferret > What it does
(project, Oct 2026 (approx.), role: solo)

- Indexes text, images, PDFs, audio and video. Audio and video become segments (30 seconds and 10 seconds by default) embedded through the model's audio and video encoders, with no transcription, and stay searchable with plain text queries.
- Three search modes: semantic, keyword or hybrid. Keyword search and filter-only browsing never call the embedder, so they work offline and against a dead server.
- Filters on file kind, extension, directory, basename glob and modified time, all applied before ranking.
- Human-readable output or JSON. The JSON search contract is frozen for its Quickshell, fzf and agent clients, and every hit carries its vector, keyword and filename scores separately.
- Resumable indexing: an interrupted run keeps its finished files, and only uncommitted PDF pages are redone.

ferret > Requirements
(project, Oct 2026 (approx.), role: solo)

- An OpenAI-compatible `POST /v1/embeddings` server. Choosing a non-local backend uploads file bytes, and the command warns when that backend is in effect.
- `poppler-utils` for PDFs, `ffmpeg` for audio and video, and ImageMagick only for HEIC photos.
- A Nix flake with a NixOS module, or a plain `cargo build --release` without Nix.
- The test suite runs against a deterministic fake embedder, so it needs no network and no GPU.

# NixOS homelab

My laptop (flow) and a home server I built from used parts (home) are both Linux machines defined in a single repo of Nix/NixOS config. Every package, service, user and firewall rule is written down there, so each machine runs exactly what the config says, and any change is a diff I can read, review and roll back.

NixOS homelab > tl;dr
(project, May 2026 to present, role: solo, status: active)

- One Nix flake builds both machines, plus a live USB image that reuses the laptop's desktop modules.
- The server hosts my passwords, photos, files, the git remote for this config and my AI services, all reached through Caddy over my private Tailscale network.
- Daily timers back up the databases and service configs to a NAS, Uptime Kuma watches the services, and ntfy pushes an alert when something fails.

NixOS homelab > Why NixOS
(project, May 2026 to present, role: solo, status: active)

I used to run a Debian server with Docker Compose and a separate local AI setup. Both drifted. Packages piled up, manual fixes stacked on each other, and neither machine could be rebuilt from scratch.

NixOS fixes that because the whole system is declared in files. A rebuild turns those files into the running system, a failed build never goes live, and every switch becomes a new generation I can go back to. Since the config lives in git, the history of each machine is the history of the repo, so I can see what changed, when, and why.

NixOS homelab > The two machines
(project, May 2026 to present, role: solo, status: active)

- **home**, the server, is built from used desktop parts: an i5-6600K, a GTX 960 and 16 GB of RAM. It's wired, runs around the clock, and holds every service below.
- **flow**, the laptop, is an ASUS ROG Flow X16 with an RTX 4060. It runs my Hyprland desktop and serves local models through a CUDA build of llama.cpp, which the server reaches over Tailscale.

The server's modules are split by role into access, infrastructure, AI, media and monitoring, with one file per service where possible, so adding or removing a service stays a small change in one place.

NixOS homelab > What the server hosts
(project, May 2026 to present, role: solo, status: active)

What the server runs, counted from the config. Native services are the ones NixOS provides as modules, like PostgreSQL, Forgejo and Immich. Horizontal bar chart of services on the home server by category. AI 16, access 6, infrastructure 6, monitoring 4, media and other 13. Bars are split into hardened containers, other containers and native NixOS services. 28 of the 35 containers start from zero Linux capabilities and block privilege escalation.

Most services run in Docker, but each container is a systemd unit with its Docker flags written in Nix, so its capabilities, memory limit and ports are part of the reviewed config instead of a compose file on the side. Most containers start with every Linux capability dropped, add back only the ones they name, and block privilege escalation. Services NixOS already packages well, like PostgreSQL, Forgejo and Immich, run as native modules.

- **Access and files.** Vaultwarden for passwords, Immich for photos, Nextcloud with Collabora for files and documents, FileBrowser for the NAS, and Forgejo, which hosts the git remote for this config.

NixOS homelab > What the server hosts

- **AI services.** A Bifrost gateway puts local and cloud models behind one OpenAI-compatible endpoint, so Open WebUI, my trawl search server and [Campus](/knowledgebase/projects/campus.md), the AI agent I built that reads all six of my courses, all call the same place. NixOS homelab > Networking and remote access
(project, May 2026 to present, role: solo, status: active)

Everything is reached over Tailscale, with Caddy as the reverse proxy in front of every web service, and the firewall only opens SSH, DNS, the web ports and Tailscale. AdGuard Home answers DNS for the house, using encrypted upstream DNS with DNSSEC, and a small split-horizon resolver gives devices on the home network the same service names that work over Tailscale, so the same link works whether I'm home or not.

NixOS homelab > Storage and backups
(project, May 2026 to present, role: solo, status: active)

Bulk data lives on a NAS that the server mounts over SMB, including Nextcloud's files, my photos and my media. Daily timers dump PostgreSQL and back up Forgejo, Vaultwarden and the service configs to the NAS, keeping seven days of copies. Secrets are encrypted in git with sops-nix and decrypted on the server at boot, so no password sits in the repo in plain text.

NixOS homelab > Monitoring and upkeep
(project, May 2026 to present, role: solo, status: active)

Most days nothing on the server needs me. Uptime Kuma watches the services and ntfy pushes an alert when something fails, Netdata shows live resource use, and Glance is a dashboard for the services. CrowdSec reads the system and Caddy logs for intrusion attempts, and fail2ban rate-limits SSH, which only accepts keys. Systemd timers handle the routine work, like backups, restarts and cleanup, and Nix garbage-collects old generations every week.

> **NIC driver bug.** The onboard network driver dropped to 10 Mbps after link hiccups. A systemd timer now checks link speed and reloads the driver.

NixOS homelab > How changes get made
(project, May 2026 to present, role: solo, status: active)

Both profiles go through the same rebuild guard. They differ in where I step in. Two rows of six steps. Homelab profile on the server: plan with the full diff, I approve, edit and dry-build on the server, nixos-safe-rebuild, verify units, containers and endpoints, then commit and push. Flow profile on the laptop: investigate, edit, commit directly with no approval gate, nixos-safe-rebuild, I test, then squash and push. Below, what happens if the rebuild goes wrong for either profile: a wrong host target is refused, a failed build activates nothing, and a bad change can be switched back, booted from the previous generation, or reverted.

NixOS homelab > How changes get made
(project, May 2026 to present, role: solo, status: active)

Each machine has its own profile of Hermes Agent, an open-source AI agent from Nous Research, and it changes the system the same way I do, by editing the config and rebuilding. It never changes a running system by hand. The server holds my data, so its profile plans first, shows me the full diff and waits for my approval, then checks that the affected units, containers and endpoints actually came back before it reports success. The laptop is only mine and most of its changes are to the desktop, where I can see right away whether they worked, so its profile commits directly and asks me to test.

Both rebuild through `nixos-safe-rebuild`, a small wrapper that refuses to build a config for a different machine than the one it runs on. Most of what I ask the agents are questions, like how something works or whether an idea is feasible. When I hand the server agent a self-hostable project, it writes the module, adds the Caddy route and rebuilds.

(project, May 2026 to present, role: solo, status: active)

I first started building my own agent just for NixOS config ([AgntOS](https://github.com/HasNate618/AgntOS)), but I wanted to be on NixOS already, so I moved both machines over and ran Hermes Agent on them instead.

NixOS homelab > Guardrails
(project, May 2026 to present, role: solo, status: active)

Each fix became config instead of a note to be careful. Incidents and dates come from the agents' own reports; each guardrail is in the public repo. Table of five incidents and the guardrails they led to. June 5, server: a security audit found plaintext and hardcoded passwords, so secrets moved to sops-nix. June, server: a dead VPN peer took the server offline until a reboot, so the VPN moved into one isolated container. Server: building the laptop's config on the server ran it out of memory, so nixos-safe-rebuild refuses any target but the current machine. Laptop: Docker auto-prune would have deleted the Windows VM's disk, so auto-prune is off on the laptop. October 12, laptop: a large Nix build exhausted RAM and froze the laptop, so build jobs are capped at 4, with earlyoom and systemd-oomd.

Most of the rules in this config came from something going wrong once. The pattern is the same every time: find the cause, then put the fix in the config so it can't happen again by accident.

NixOS homelab > What I learned
(project, May 2026 to present, role: solo, status: active)

- Declaring the whole system pays off the first time something breaks, because the fix is a diff I can read, keep and roll back instead of a manual change I'd have to remember.
- A declarative system is also the right surface for an agent. Its output is a diff, and the build checks that diff before anything changes.
- Autonomy should match what's at stake, so the same agent software runs looser on my laptop than on the server that holds my data.
